BREZGI

A chronicle of one spot of earth · Taurenes pagasts · Vidzeme · Latvija

This is an interpretive reconstruction of a landscape. The modern elevation model, mapped water and historical maps anchor every view. They cannot show the exact ancient drainage, or individual buildings, trees, people and graves, so those are reconstructed. The central family farm is a staged viewpoint near Taurene, and the actual Brezģis settlement lies farther south. Each era's story ends with a note on its evidence.

The modern scene is labelled 2025, although it combines a 2020 Sentinel-2 mosaic with 2026 OpenStreetMap data. Building heights, tree positions, the depths of rivers and lakes, and the designs of bus shelters are inferred. A mapped place today says nothing certain about how an object there looked in an earlier era.

This is a real square of the Vidzeme Upland, 8.8 kilometres on each side. It runs south from Taurene village to Brezģis and Brežģa kalns in the old Cēsis district. The ground is the actual elevation model of that square [18]. The Gauja, its brooks and its lakes follow their mapped courses and shores [19]. Dabaru ezers, which the young Gauja flows through beside the village, was also recovered from the flat lake surface in the elevation data [4]. The Gauja is newborn here. It threads a chain of seven glacial lakes called Bānūžu, Ilzes, Rijas, Brenkūžu, Stupēnu, Dabaru and Taurenes [4]. On the hill west of Dabaru ezers stands Lejstupu pilskalns, a state-protected hillfort and one of thirteen registered archaeological monuments in this single parish [10]. In the simulation it stands exactly where it really is.

The name Brezgis

Three facts lead to one careful inference. First, six kilometres south of the village lies the settlement of Brezģis, which was also known as Brežģa krogs, the Brezga tavern. In the nineteenth century the manor brewery sold its ale there [2][4]. Second, beside it rises Brežģa kalns, which at 255.4 m is the highest point in the parish. The long ridge has an oak on its summit, and it forces the Gauja into a great loop toward Taurene. In independent Latvia it was the parish's festival hill, with Jāņi bonfires every midsummer and open-air theatre from 1937 to 1939, until the Soviet army arrived in 1940 [7][2]. Third, the peasants of Vidzeme took hereditary surnames in 1826, most often from the farm or landmark where they lived [5][6].

So a family named Brezgis may well carry the name of this place, whether the tavern, a farm or the hill. That link fits the ordinary way surnames formed in Vidzeme. Even so, no published genealogy found for this project documents it. The simulated family farm sits near the village core so that the manor, the river and the school can be seen together. Meanwhile the real Brezģis settlement and Brežģa kalns lie in the southern part of the map, up the valley.

~10,800 BC · After the ice

The oldest scene shows the youngest land. The ice sheet had withdrawn, but its dead remains still lay buried in the hollows of this moraine country. Some of those stranded blocks melted thousands of years later into the very lakes the parish is braided around. In western Latvia, kettle holes were still collapsing into ponds around 8500 to 7400 cal BP [21]. The scene is set in the Younger Dryas, on treeless tundra of dwarf birch, juniper and sedge, with glacial erratics, reindeer and meltwater. Leaving people out is an interpretive choice. In fact, Latvia's earliest known inhabitants were Late Palaeolithic reindeer hunters [22], and someone may well have crossed this terrace. The modern terrain serves as the reference for every era, so the river and lake shores of the Younger Dryas are approximate.

~AD 50 · Where the aurochs grazed

In the Early Iron Age the upland was nearly wilderness. Pollen studies show that woodland persisted through the whole Iron Age, and the human traces here are mostly graves, such as Finnic stone tarand graves and Baltic sand barrows [13][15]. The camp on the terrace is a seasonal hunters' shelter. Then there are the aurochs. Taurs is the Latvian word for the wild ox, and Latvian linguistics counts place names like Taurene as evidence that the animals lived in these woods [16]. By then they were rare, since the species was retreating toward its last strongholds in Lithuania, East Prussia and Poland, where the final cow died in 1627 [17]. Still, a herd on a Vidzeme river meadow in AD 50 is defensible. The herd grazes the same terrace where the farm will one day stand, kur tauri ganījās. The bulls are nearly black with a pale stripe down the back, and the cows are red-brown, just as the species is described. The elk at the forest edge were always here.

~AD 950 · A Latgalian farmstead

By the Late Iron Age this was Latgalian country [13]. The farmstead is built on the finest archaeological evidence in the Baltic, the lake fortress of Āraiši, 25 km to the west. Its timbers were felled in AD 835, a date fixed to the single year by the cosmic-ray spike of AD 774/5 in their tree rings [11]. From Āraiši come the small log dwellings of about 30 m² with a clay stove at the centre. The same site gives the bark roofs weighted with poles, the granary raised on posts, a resident bronze caster, rye, barley and turnips, and forest beekeeping [11][12]. The animals are small on purpose. The cattle stand about a metre high, the forest horses are pony-sized, the sheep are dark and primitive, and there are only a few chickens, which had newly arrived in the eastern Baltic [14]. The fields are līdumi, clearings burnt out of the forest and sown between the stumps. Across the river, the palisaded refuge on Lejstupu hill stands on a documented hillfort site [10]. The farm, the burial mounds and the offerings follow regional evidence. However, their exact places here and the look of the hillfort in the ninth century are unknown.

1860 · Brezgi under Nēķene manor

The parish is now Nēķene, or Nötkenshof, named for the Notken family who took the estate in 1601. Since 1856 the von Panders have been its lords [2][3]. Serfdom ended in Vidzeme in 1819, and it brought freedom without land. Surnames followed in 1826, and within a decade families like this one began buying their farms [5][6]. The farmstead is the classic viensēta, checked detail by detail against the Vidzeme homestead at the Ethnographic Open-Air Museum [8]. There is the dwelling with its first chimney and small glass panes, and the great thatched rija, whose thatch the grain smoke preserved. There is the shingled and locked klēts, the long windowless byre and the pirts smoking by the river on Saturday. Around them stand the well sweep, the slanted riķu fence, log beehives, hay on poles and the orchard.

Across the fields, the old classicist manor house watches from its linden park. On the bank below, the manor brewery cooled 25,000 buckets of ale a year in three stone cellars vaulted into the slope of the Gauja, and it sold the ale at the Brezgi tavern [2]. In 1905, when revolution burned the manors all around, Nēķena survived because its own peasants stood against the arsonists, to the Panders' credit. Nevertheless, the next year the tsarist court-martial turned those cellars into a prison [2][3]. The manor also keeps a gentler legend about a White Lady who dances through the buildings on nights of the full moon. A low weir holds the Gauja up into a mill pond below the manor, where the 1930s Army map shows one, although the mill itself is not documented.

1935 · Taurene

The agrarian reform of 1920 took the manors. Nēķena's fields alone became 72 new farms, and the German aristocrats left [9][3]. In 1925 the schoolteacher Kārlis Bormanis (1877 to 1958) persuaded the parish council to revive the name of the medieval Tauren estate. He was born in this parish, taught at the Taurene school and wrote Zeme, Latvia's first school geography textbook. The new name was Taurene, from taurs, the aurochs, and it took effect on New Year's Day 1926 [1][2][3]. The parish arms bear aurochs horns to this day [2]. The phrase "where the aurochs once grazed" survives as local tradition, since no written quote from Bormanis has been found. He was more a schoolmaster than a poet. Even so, the poetry came anyway.

Kur tu skriesi, tauriņ mans?
Uz Taureni, uz Taureni!
Māra Zālīte, quoted for the parish decades later [20]

In the scene, the brick new manor stands beside the older palace, which the parish took over as a clinic [3]. The new manor's roof raising was celebrated in 1888, and its architect was R. G. Šmēlings. The farm has a shingle roof, framed windows and a porch. Telephone poles follow the gravel road, and the stork keeps its nest on an old wheel. On Jāņi night fires burn on the hills, most famously on Brežģa kalns itself, every midsummer until 1940 [7][2]. The aurochs are centuries gone, yet they live on in the name.

2025 · Taurene today

The modern era wears real satellite colours. Sentinel-2 cloudless imagery is draped over the terrain, woodland is estimated from the imagery, and individual trees are generated procedurally [23]. Taurene village and Taurenes parish cover different areas, so their population totals cannot be read as a single decline [4][3]. The manor ensemble still houses the parish's civic life. South along the old road, past the site of Brežģa krogs, stands the eleven-metre observation tower on Brežģa kalns. It was raised in 2017 and looks out over Alauksts and the lake chain [7][24]. The Jāņi fire still burns beside it every midsummer.

The map that checked this world

These are two windows from the 1930s Latvian Army map at 1 to 75,000, the survey that the 1935 era was checked against farm by farm. The left one shows the village core, with Nēķina mž. (the manor), the parish hall (Pag. vld.), the mill pond on the Gauja, and the Dabari and Leistupni farms that this simulation places on the same ground. The right one shows Brežģa kalns and the old Cēsis to Vecpiebalga road climbing past the tavern, which is the family's country.

The sheet is the Latvijas Armijas topogrāfiskā karte at 1 to 75,000, a state survey of the 1920s and 1930s in the public domain, with tiles from vesture.dodies.lv. Its elevations are in sazhens, so multiply them by 2.134 to get metres. The land cover of the 2025 era comes from Sentinel-2 cloudless imagery (EOX, CC-BY 4.0), and the parish coat of arms with the gold aurochs of Taurene is the official municipal blazon.

What is real and what is interpretation

Real, from data. The terrain [18], the Gauja, the lakes and brooks [19], Dabaru ezers in its true place [4] and the location of the hillfort [10] all come from data.

Documented, then reconstructed. The Āraiši-type buildings and bark roofs [11][12], the set of viensēta buildings [8], the manor ensemble, brewery and park [2][3], the livestock species and sizes [14], the burial customs [13], the renaming [1][3], and Brežģa kalns with its fires [7] are all documented and then reconstructed with interpretation.

Interpretive licence. The simulated farmstead stays at the village core so that the manor, the river and the school share one view. The real Brezgi ground, the tavern site and Brežģa kalns are on the map as well, six kilometres south along the old road. The watermill is typical for a Gauja manor, while the yard layouts and the weather are our own. No people are shown. Instead the village keeps their traces, such as smoke, laundry on the line, a loaded cart and an axe left in the block.

Keys 1 to 6 travel in time. The walking button drops you to eye level, where WASD moves, Shift runs and Space jumps, and the same button returns you to flight. The sun dial in the corner sets the time of day. Evening brings the long midsummer dusk, with fireflies over the meadow and the Jāņi bonfire on Brežģa kalns, and in the ice age it brings the aurora. The camera feel, the wind model and several realism standards are adapted from LAAS, an MIT-licensed procedural world engine [25], and the terrain detail, water reflections and physical sky follow its example.

Built with three.js on the real terrain of Taurene. Research notes with full citations live alongside the project. It was made for the Brezgis family as cultural memory, honestly sourced.
